Data investigation RNPDNO Mexico

The Redacted Crisis

What Mexico's public registry leaves unseen

On 15 August 2026 Mexico's official registry counted 134,268 people still missing. Its live dashboard publishes only totals. In the last record-level snapshot, dated 2 December 2025, 36.8% of unresolved records revealed only two things: the state, and which office filed the report. Ten snapshots taken between April and December 2025 show that this blackout does not move one family at a time. It moves in batches — about 2,500 records in one state in two months — and in several states the share hidden differs by 30 to 60 points depending on which office filed the case.

Two descriptive fields survive, plus an anonymous record ID; birth date, registration date and municipality code are also withheld.

1

The crisis is real, and it is growing

Start with the honest version of the number. On 15 August 2026 Mexico's National Registry of Disappeared and Missing Persons (RNPDNO) contained 407,253 records: 249,502 people recorded as found alive, 23,483 found dead and 134,268 still missing Source [1]. Those are current registry statuses, not dates on which anybody was found.

Figure A looks at the subset assigned a year of disappearance between 2000 and 2025. Across those cohorts the registry currently records roughly 214,600 found alive, 20,600 found dead and 117,100 still missing. The gap between those figures and the headline totals consists mainly of records without a usable year and records outside the chart's period.

Three things stand out.

  • The yearly cohorts have grown more than tenfold in eighteen years. The registry holds about 3,000 records for 2007, the year the militarised drug war began, and 37,124 for 2025 Source [1]. That is growth in the registry, which is not the same thing as growth in disappearances — see the next figure.
  • A third of the people in it are still missing. 134,268 of 407,253. Since 2015 the still-missing share of each year's cohort has stayed between 29% and 38%, while the cohorts themselves kept growing.
  • The registry's red band never really empties. Most cohorts since 2012 now sit roughly two-thirds in a "located" category — 75% of 2014, 68% of 2025 — though not all: the 2010 and 2011 cohorts are only 45% and 54% located. In every cohort a large unresolved remainder stays where it is.

Now the limits, because they change what those numbers mean.

Each bar counts records the state holds, not disappearances that happened. Over 25 years, reporting rates, prosecutorial practice and registry coverage all changed enormously, and cases still arrive late: Data Cívica found that the registry's count of disappearances up to July 2024 grew by 14,952 records between its July 2024 consultation and a July 2026 re-extraction Source [10]. The cohorts have also had wildly unequal time to resolve — 2008 has been observed for eighteen years, 2025 for months — so the two-thirds figure describes where the register stands today, not how effectively anyone searched.

And "located" is a registry category, not a verified outcome. It mixes people found alive, people found dead, and records reclassified in administrative batches, including the contested 2023 censo. The public data cannot tell you when a status changed or why: someone recorded in the 2014 cohort may have been found that year or a decade later. Nothing here credits any institution with finding anyone.

(The 2000–2005 bars look dramatic in percentage form but cover only a few hundred records each, so the piece draws no trend from them.)

2

But is the country more violent, or better at recording?

A tenfold rise invites one obvious reading — that the country simply became more violent — and for a decade the data support it. Between 2015 and 2018 recorded disappearances and homicide victims climb together.

Then they part. From 2019 to 2024, homicide victims fall 13.4%, from 34,721 to 30,060, while recorded disappearances rise 43.4%, from 25,151 to 36,056. With only ten complete years, a correlation coefficient adds little here: the two series correlate at about r = 0.53 over 2015–2024, a value that ten trending points cannot distinguish from no relationship, and their year-to-year changes are essentially uncorrelated. The plain comparison is the evidence: after 2019 the lines move in opposite directions. Two further cautions apply. The disappearance series counts people by the year they went missing, as registered by August 2026, while homicide victims are counted when an investigation is opened; and 2025 is provisional in both. On national totals, worsening lethal violence does not account for the registry's recent growth.

Part of the answer is that the country built the machinery to record more. The 2017 General Law created local search commissions. Among unresolved records with public fields in the 2025-12-02 mirror, 5.0% of cases for 2017 came through a search commission, against 47.7% for 2025, while the prosecutors' share fell from 94% to 45%; the CNB's online reporting portal, launched in late 2019, accounts for 8% to 21% of each cohort since 2020 Source [3]. A family that once had to persuade a prosecutor now has somewhere else to go. Crucially, this breakdown applies only to unresolved records whose fields are public (63.2% of the mirror snapshot); neither the confidential records nor resolved cases can be assumed to follow the same intake pattern. That exclusion bites hardest exactly where the shift happens: Data Cívica's analysis of a February 2026 extract found more confidential than public records for the 2021–2023 cohorts Source [10].

This does not make the rise an illusion. Two official series moving apart is a fact about the two series; falling homicides say nothing about how honestly disappearances are recorded, and a disappearance is not a homicide. But it does mean the tenfold figure cannot be read as a measure of how much worse the violence became. It measures a registry — one whose reach and rules both changed inside the period it covers.

There is a darker reading of the same divergence: that deaths are being recorded as disappearances, so the homicide statistic improves without anything improving. The registry's outcome split weighs against that as the whole explanation, but it cannot rule it out.

The 2024 cohort is 10,905 records larger than the 2019 cohort. 61.7% of that difference is people the registry now records as found alive — 6,732 more than in 2019 — which a relabelling of homicides could not produce. But 36.8% of the difference, 4,017 records, is people still missing, and that is exactly where an uncounted killing would sit. Over the same years homicide victims fell by 4,661. Add homicide victims to the registry's still-missing count and the total barely moves — 42,970 in 2019, 42,326 in 2024. That proves no substitution, but it leaves room for some. The found-dead difference, 156, cannot settle it either way: the 2024 cohort has had two years to be identified, the 2019 cohort seven.

What this cannot rule out is quieter and more troubling, and it has two forms. A body that is never found enters neither statistic — not the homicide count, because no victim is ever named, and not the registry's found-dead column, because nobody is ever found. That channel is real, and Teuchitlán is what it looks like when one instance of it surfaces.

The second form is not unmeasured at all. Between 2006 and 2023, 72,172 bodies entered Mexico's forensic services and were never given a name back Source [6]. Two thirds of them, 48,108, were sent to cemetery common graves. Nearly a fifth — 13,272 — have been unidentified for more than a decade. These people were found. They are in the state's own custody. And because nobody knows who they are, they cannot be matched to anyone in the registry, so they sit in neither the found-dead column nor, in most cases, anywhere a searching family can reach. The count is a floor, not a total: the Fiscalía of Morelos declined to answer the transparency requests, and the figure counts whole bodies, not the bone fragments that clandestine graves mostly yield.

So the gap between the two series on this chart is not simply unknown. Part of it has already been counted — compiled by journalists from the state's own forensic services, rather than published by the state. The claim this section can defend stays narrow — most of the registry's recent growth is not the homicide count in disguise, though a partial shift cannot be excluded — and the reason the two counts fail to meet is partly a forensic backlog with a number attached to it.

---

3

Where unresolved stock is greatest per resident

Mexico's disappeared are not distributed the way Mexicans are. Estado de México and Mexico City register the most cases in absolute terms, which is unsurprising: they are where the most people live. Divide by population and the map rearranges itself.

The national rate is 98 unresolved records per 100,000 residents, counting the 130,602 records assigned to a state; another 2,964 name no state. Tamaulipas, on the northeastern border, runs at 359 — more than four times Estado de México's 82. Behind it come Zacatecas (226) and Sinaloa (211). This is a map of the unresolved registry stock, not of underlying risk: differences in reporting, resolution and publication practice all affect where a state appears.

This is the ordinary way to read registry data, and for one paragraph it works. Hold onto it. The next chart takes it apart.

4

The wall: one in three records is blank

Here is what "consulting the public registry" actually gets you: for 36.8% of unresolved records, every descriptive field is redacted — no date, no age, no sex, no municipality, no case status. Two facts survive: the state, and the name of the authority that filed the report. This is why national trend charts and state comparisons are built on different denominators, and why every chart in this piece says so.

The top of this ranking is the easier half to read. The bottom is the trap. A state sits low here when it redacts little of what it holds — which says nothing at all about how much it holds. Guerrero's 9.1% is the lowest bar on the chart and the weakest evidence of openness in this piece; §8 is about why.

The redaction is not evenly spread. Jalisco redacts two of every three records. Guerrero, one of the most violent states in the country, redacts one in eleven.

5

State violence does not explain confidentiality

There is an innocent explanation for all this redaction, and it deserves a fair test. The law itself supplies it: Article 108 lets families ask that a record not be made public "for reasons of security" Source [4].

If statewide danger were the principal explanation for interstate variation in confidentiality, states with higher homicide rates should generally redact more.

The data do not show that pattern. Across all 32 states, the correlation between the confidential share and the cumulative homicide-victim rate for 2015–2025 is negative — Pearson r = −0.38 Source [2]. That value leans on Colima and weakens to −0.28 without it, so the robust finding is the absence of any positive relationship, not the negative one. Several of the most violent states are among those publishing the largest share of registry detail. Colima has recorded roughly 950 homicides per 100,000 residents since 2015, the highest rate in the country; it redacts 9% of its disappearance records. Guerrero, at 550, redacts 9%. Chihuahua, at 548, redacts 9%.

At the other end of the scale, Jalisco's homicide rate is less than half Guerrero's and it redacts 67%. Yucatán has both the lowest homicide rate and the lowest unresolved-record rate in Mexico — 18 and 12.5 per 100,000 respectively — yet redacts 62% of its records.

The narrow conclusion, and the only one this supports: state-level homicide rates do not explain state-level differences in confidentiality. This is an ecological comparison between states; it does not measure risk in any individual case, and it cannot rule out case-by-case risk assessments, which no public field records. What it does rule out is the simplest version of the official rationale — that redaction tracks danger — as the explanation for why Jalisco sits at 67% and Guerrero at 9%.

So what does account for the difference?

6

Who decides a record goes dark

On paper, the rule is humane and simple. Article 108 of the General Law on Disappearances lets families ask, for security reasons, that their loved one's information be kept out of the public registry, and requires that families be told of their data rights before giving information. Redaction, officially, means "the family asked."

The government's own paperwork says otherwise. In August 2020 the National Search Commission (CNB) wrote to the transparency institute (INAI) asking how to build the public registry — and admitted, in its own tables, that for 77.4% of records nobody knew whether the family had consented or not — which the CNB attributed, "probably and among other factors," to many records predating the law. In the proceedings that followed, the CNB argued that without families' express consent it could not release the data — and when a journalist asked for the consent declarations it was relying on, it answered that they did not exist Source [4]. And in a footnote, the CNB recorded that the Fiscalía of Jalisco had declared that everything it sends to the national registry is non-publishable, invoking family refusals without producing any supporting documentation in the public proceeding.

When INAI ordered the CNB to release a public database (resolution RRA 09082/20, and at least two later resolutions), the commission resisted on those grounds and eventually delivered 50,204 records against the 175,371 then registered — about 29% Source [4].

There is a simpler reason the consent paperwork is missing, and it is visible in the registry's own fields. When Data Cívica audited the public version the CNB published in August 2023 — 110,964 records — it found that the contact details of the person who reported the disappearance had been left blank in seven of every ten cases Source [7]. That is the field an authority would need in order to ask a family anything at all. Lawyers at Centro Prodh report families who gave their details to authorities in 2017 and 2020 and were never entered into the system, and put the consequence plainly: it ends up looking as though the families are the ones who withheld the information. A registry that did not record how to reach seven families in ten cannot then explain its silence by saying the families did not speak.

The one field the registry leaves on a confidential record makes a test possible: it names the office that filed the report. If redaction reflected what families chose, it should not depend much on which office happened to take the case. In several states it depends on it enormously. In Estado de México, 3% of the unresolved records filed by state prosecutors are confidential, against 36% of those filed by the state's search commission. In Nuevo León the figures are 32% and 93%; in Jalisco, 64% and 90%. The gap does not even run the same way everywhere — in Puebla and Baja California Sur it is the prosecutors who redact more — which is itself the finding: no single rule is being applied. In six of the 17 states where both offices filed enough cases to compare, the two differ by 30 points or more; in eight, by fewer than 10. Families who report directly through the national commission's online portal, meanwhile, end up confidential at a similar rate almost everywhere, between about 35% and 41% across the middle half of the states with enough cases to measure Source [3]. This is a description, not a proof: the channels do not receive identical cases, and the portal leans toward family self-reports and recent years. But family preferences do not obviously change at an office door. Office practice plainly does.

Journalists then closed the loop. In 2024, ZonaDocs found 4,765 cases across six states that are marked confidential in the registry while having active public search notices — posters with names and photographs. In transparency responses reported by ZonaDocs, authorities said they produce no context or risk analysis for these publication decisions, arguing the law does not require one. María de Jesús Solís, whose son disappeared in Zapopan in 2020, said she never signed for his record to be confidential and wants maximum visibility. Her son's record is confidential Source [4].

The redaction flag mixes genuine family requests, missing consent paperwork and at least one blanket declaration by a state prosecutor's office — and no public field distinguishes them.

6b

The totals move in batches

If confidentiality were updated one family decision at a time, we might expect it to move gradually. Instead the published count sometimes jumps. Tamaulipas added ~2,500 confidential records in two months (May–July 2025) while its total barely moved; its redaction share went from 20% to 39%, and every chart in this piece would have looked different had we pulled the data in April. Jalisco's confidential count drifted down for most of the year, then fell by about 1,200 in the last quarter as the state's overall federal count also fell — before the new recount was announced in January 2026. Tabasco's published total fell by a third in a single month. Data Cívica, comparing re-extractions a year apart, found that falls of this kind in Jalisco and Tabasco were roughly matched by rises in records marked located — while noting it cannot confirm they are the same records Source [10].

The reversals do not stop at the edge of the panel. Mexico City's unresolved count climbed steadily all through 2025, from 6,025 in April to 7,242 in December — and then gave the entire increase back. By August 2026 the live registry showed 5,915: a capital that had been adding cases for a year shed 1,327 of them in eight months, roughly one in five. We can see the direction and the size of that reversal but not its mechanism: the registry does not say whether those records were deleted, reclassified, resolved, or moved.

6c

"Located" is a status the register asserts

For one episode, that question has been answered — and not by the registry.

In August 2023 the National Search Commission published a person-level version of the register containing 110,964 names. In December, after the federal government's Estrategia Nacional de Búsqueda Generalizada — the censo — the equivalent public version held 94,283. Data Cívica compared the two and found 10,953 names present in the first and absent from the second Source [8]. The official explanation for the smaller register was that people had been located in house-to-house visits Source [8]. Data Cívica is careful about what its own method can establish: those names should belong to people who were located, and if they do not, the person has been disappeared a second time. The comparison can show that a name left the register; it cannot show whether the person was found, is alive, or is safe.

Quinto Elemento Lab tested the other side of the same operation. Of the 16,681 people the censo declared located, it reconstructed 11,026 names — at least 4,607 more were published redacted — and crossed them against missing-persons lists held by collectives, the FGR's own ¿Has visto a...? search notices, the UN Committee on Enforced Disappearances' urgent actions, and dirty-war case files. That produced 85 candidates. Ten journalists then contacted families and accompanying collectives one by one, and confirmed 30 people who were listed as located and had not come home Source [9]. Nine more had recent search reports the team could not confirm directly. Two had been erased from the register altogether.

The individual cases show how a location gets recorded. Miguel Ángel Hernández Guzmán disappeared in Orizaba, Veracruz, in May 2019, at 27. The men who took him are serving sentences for kidnapping and forced disappearance and have not returned him; the FGR still circulates a notice asking whether anyone has seen him; the censo lists him as located. His mother, Lorena Guzmán, searches clandestine graves. "It is not true that my son has been located," she told the reporters. "That is a lie." José Marco Antonio Márquez Sandoval was recorded as located on the strength of a DNA match to a single arm bone, which his family disputes, and then removed from the register entirely. "I do not accept my son as found because of a piece of arm bone they found," said his mother, Leticia Sandoval Zúñiga.

The reporters also obtained the call log behind the census visits: more than 18,000 calls placed from a federal call centre in October 2023, of which over 86% went unanswered. In four documented cases officials recorded either that nobody answered or that the family said their relative had not come back — and all four folios appear on the located list.

Thirty confirmed cases out of 16,681 is not proof that the census was fabricated, and this piece does not claim it was. What those thirty establish is narrower and harder to argue with: "located" is a status the register can assert without verifying it. The Interior Secretary, Luisa María Alcalde, said the locations would still have to be validated, but also that for the 16,681 the government had "certainty of their whereabouts" Source [9]. The thirty documented cases contradict that certainty. Karla Quintana, who left the National Search Commission months after the census was announced, has accused the exercise of aiming "to reduce the figures of disappeared people, mainly under this government" Source [9].

The exercise has a successor. On 27 March 2026 the federal government presented the 132,534 people then recorded as missing in three operational groups: 46,742 records it said lacked the data needed to search, 40,308 showing administrative activity after the disappearance — among which it said it had confirmed 5,338 locations — and 43,128 with no activity at all Source [11]. Data Cívica, working from a February 2026 extract, found that fewer than 2% of records lack the combination of name, dates and other fields needed to identify a person Source [10]. The same pattern holds: a status is asserted for tens of thousands of records at once, and the public cannot check it record by record.

Step changes, flat totals during reclassification, batch removals: these patterns are consistent with administrative processing — records handled in bulk, by an office, on an office's schedule. They are not proof that the underlying consent decisions are fabricated. Families do decide, and some of those decisions are surely real; a backlog of genuine consent forms entered in one batch would look much like this from the outside. But the census shows what bulk processing can produce when it is not checked afterwards, and it is the only episode in this period we know of in which anyone outside did check. What the shape of the data does show is that the timing of publication is governed by administrative operations rather than by when families decide, and that the two cannot be separated from the public record.

That is the version-history counterpart to section 6. Together they support a claim that is narrower than "the state is hiding people" and harder to dismiss: the registry's most basic public property — how much of it you can read — is rewritten in bulk, state by state, with no public log we could find of who authorised a change or why, and no field that distinguishes a redaction a family asked for from one that a missing form produced.

7

Jalisco: opacity by redaction

Jalisco redacts more of its registry than any other state in Mexico: 9,216 of its 13,766 unresolved records, two out of every three. It is also the state that stopped fully participating in the national count.

From 2022, under then-governor Enrique Alfaro, Jalisco largely stopped reporting disappearances to the RNPDNO and logged them in its own state registry instead. The country now has two official counts of Jalisco's disappeared, kept by two governments, and they do not agree with each other. By the article's own comparison of public snapshots, the resulting gap now reaches roughly 3,000 people — following earlier divergence documented by El Informador Source [4]. Accused of erasing records, the state government answered in January 2024 with a communiqué titled "Jalisco does not manipulate its registry, nor erase figures" Source [4].

Jalisco is also where the contradiction from section 6 concentrates. Of the 4,765 confidential-yet-publicly-searched-for cases ZonaDocs identified, 1,026 are Jalisco's — second only to Estado de México's 2,691 — equal to about a ninth of the 9,216 Jalisco records marked confidential in December 2025, though ZonaDocs counted at an earlier date. The same investigation reports a further 2,137 disappearances between 2019 and mid-2024 that were never registered federally — by its account not redacted inside the national count, but absent from it Source [4].

What the registry did not record, families recorded themselves. On 5 March 2025 the collective Guerreros Buscadores de Jalisco entered Rancho Izaguirre, a property outside Teuchitlán, and found what the collective described as an extermination site and what the federal Attorney General later described as a cartel recruitment centre: clothing, shoes, backpacks, notebooks, bone fragments Source [4]. It became a national scandal — not only for what was on the ranch, but because the National Guard had raided the same property six months earlier, in September 2024, and it took a group of searching families to document what was there Source [4].

Searching in Jalisco carries mortal risk. In March 2025 Teresa González Murillo, who was searching for her brother, was shot at her home in Guadalajara; she died days later. In April 2025 María del Carmen Morales, of Guerreros Buscadores, was shot dead in Tlajomulco with one of her sons; she had been searching for another. In both cases prosecutors listed the victims' search work among their lines of investigation; no motive has been established in court Source [12].

The state with the most redacted registry in Mexico is also the state where civil society keeps producing the evidence its registry lacks. They may not be two separate facts about Jalisco, but one fact seen from two sides.

8

Guerrero: the limits of official counts

On the redaction chart, Guerrero appears unusually open: 9% confidential, against Jalisco's 67%. But a low confidential share describes only records that have entered the federal stock. It cannot tell us how completely the registry covers disappearances known to families and collectives.

In 2022 reporting, the human-rights centre Tlachinollan documented roughly 3,800 records in Guerrero's state registry; in the federal 2025-12-02 mirror snapshot, unresolved records for the state reached 4,453. In Iguala alone — one city — three family collectives jointly document 623 cases.

Those numbers are not a subtraction, and it matters that we say so. They may overlap, and we cannot measure by how much. Some of the 623 Iguala cases are certainly also registered with the state; others, by the collectives' account, are not. Without case-level identifiers on both sides — which no public source provides — there is no way to net one against the other. The comparison is worth making because of the ratio it implies: three collectives in one city hold a caseload equal to a seventh of the federal register (and a sixth of the 2022 state count). It is not worth making as an estimate of how many people are missing from that register.

The human-rights centre Tlachinollan, which has tracked the state for decades, describes prosecutors who stall investigations unless families force them open, and a forensic service that has effectively collapsed. In Guerrero it documents that between 2% and 6% of disappearance cases are ever prosecuted. Nationally, the CNB counted 36 sentences for forced disappearance by the end of 2021 Source [4].

The modern searching-mothers movement was, in an important sense, born here. When the 43 students from Ayotzinapa disappeared in September 2014, families searching the hills around Iguala for them began instead to find other people: graves of the dead nobody was officially looking for. The collective that formed out of that search, Los Otros Desaparecidos de Iguala, has since exhumed more than 160 bodies. Tlachinollan credits women-led collectives — not state institutions — with the recovery of 260 bodies in Iguala, of which 69 were identified and returned to their families. In Acapulco it records a different outcome: 70 people found alive, and 55 identified bodies returned Source [4].

The gap is not history. During Holy Week searches in 2026, in Buenavista de Cuéllar and Iguala, eight families approached searching mothers from the collective Familiares en Búsqueda María Herrera — five in Buenavista and three in Iguala — to report disappearances. One woman in Iguala whose father had been missing six months recounted that authorities had reported no progress and told her to stop coming by — they would let her know if they found anything Source [4]. That is the gap happening in real time: families bringing their cases to search collectives — at least one of them after official channels had stalled.

A low confidential share, then, is not a clean bill of health. Jalisco documents how fields can disappear after a record enters the registry. Guerrero's family records show why coverage before that point must be investigated separately. The project cannot measure Guerrero's under-registration from these sources because the official and collective lists have not been linked person by person.

9

What this means — and what we cannot claim

No chart in this piece supports the sentence "the state deliberately hides its disappeared." I looked for it and could not find it, and the honest reason is that the public data are not built to answer questions about intent. Every explanation that could be tested from outside, state by state — that redaction tracks how dangerous a state is, that it tracks corruption, that it tracks state poverty — found no support. None of those tests can see inside an individual case. What is left is not proof of a motive. It is the absence of an account that survives testing.

That absence is the finding, and it is specific. The confidentiality flag is unexplained record by record, never officially audited in any public source we found, and contradicted in thousands of documented cases by public search notices. It moves in batches, on what look like administrative schedules, with no public log we could find of who authorised a change or why. And no public field distinguishes a redaction a family requested from one produced by a missing form — which means the public record cannot show that the humane version of its own rule is what is happening, even where it is.

The practical consequence for anyone using this data: a cross-state comparison of the RNPDNO measures institutional publication practice at least as much as it measures disappearance. Jalisco redacts seven times as much of its register as Guerrero while recording less than half Guerrero's homicide rate — the publication gap runs opposite to the violence gap, not alongside it. Any map, ranking or model built on those numbers without saying so is describing bureaucracies while appearing to describe victims.

And there are two different ways to vanish from the record, which the same chart cannot show at once: fields redacted inside the registry, and people never entered into it. The first is measurable — we measured it. The second is visible only where families have done the counting themselves, and the registry publishes no identifiers that would let anyone reconcile the two. Guerrero's 623 documented Iguala cases and its ~3,800 official records cannot be added, subtracted, or matched. That is not a gap in our method. It is a gap in what the public record contains.

Which leaves the part no dataset in this piece can reach. Behind 134,268 records is a number of families who learned that the search would be theirs to run — and who, in Iguala and Teuchitlán and dozens of places with no reporters in them, went out with rods and shovels and found what the registry does not contain. Counting what they have found, and at what cost, is the subject of the next piece.

---

Methods and limits

This piece draws on two data vintages that cannot be merged, and every figure is labelled with the one it uses. They answer different questions and carry different cutoff dates. Reading a number from one against a number from the other will give a wrong answer.

[1] Aggregate outcomes — vintage 2026-08-15 (live). All-record totals and the by-year outcome breakdown in fig A. Source: RNPDNO public dashboard, captured 2026-08-15 23:49 America/Mexico_City. Covers every record including confidential ones, because the dashboard counts records it will not display. Totals: 407,253 records — 249,502 recorded found alive, 23,483 found dead, 134,268 disappeared or not located. Frozen with source hashes at data/publication_freezes/2026-08-15/. ↩

[2] Homicide and state-capacity variables — vintage 2015–2025. SESNSP homicide victims: aggregated 2015–2025 per 100,000 and matched to all 32 states for the correlations in §5 and the negative controls in docs/methodology.md §7; and as a national annual series for fig I, where the file's January 2015 start sets that chart's start year and its October 2025 end makes the final year provisional. Also INEGI ENCIG 2025 (corruption prevalence) and PIBE 2024 (GDP per capita). ↩

[3] Record-level microdata — vintage 2025-12-02 (frozen). Every field-level figure: redaction shares, per-capita rates, and the state rankings in figs B, C and D. Source: the public RNPDNO record-level extract via the lapanquecita mirror — 133,566 records, upstream commit 666b3e7605, max FECHA_REGISTRO 2025-12-01. This mirror stopped publishing after 2025-12-02, having released monthly since April 2025, and no comparable record-level extract has appeared since. Our copy is byte-identical to the last upstream commit. ↩

Drift between Source [1] and Source [3] is small nationally — the mirror's 133,566 records sit 0.5% below the live 134,268 — but larger once records with no state are set aside: 130,602 state-assigned records in the mirror against 133,416 live (−2.1%), because the mirror files 2,964 records under an unknown state against 852 live. It is not uniform by state. Ciudad de México has since fallen 18% and Jalisco 6% against the frozen microdata; both carry their live figures in the caption. src/crosscheck.py reports the full per-state drift table.

[4] Documentary and journalistic sources, each with its own date: Oficio SEGOB/CNBP/1349/2020 (consent accounting, universe dated 2020-08-07; CNB letter to INAI, obtained as a PDF and hash-pinned in the publication freeze); A dónde van los desaparecidos, 2021-04-08, on INAI resolution RRA 09082/20 (December 2020) and the two that followed it — the order to publish a public-version database, the CNB's answer that the consent declarations it cited did not exist, and the eventual delivery of 50,204 records (older RNPED files plus 11,197 newer records) against 175,371 registered; ZonaDocs, "El engaño estadístico", 2024-11-21 (active notices marked confidential; Jalisco under-registration); El Informador, 2023-05-09 (Jalisco federal/state divergence); Animal Político, 2026-02-09 (Jalisco's halt in federal reporting since 2022 and state registry divergence); Proceso, 2024-01-23 (the Jalisco government's denial); A dónde van los desaparecidos, 2026-01-08 (new federal recount announced); CNN en Español, 2025-04-29 (FGR on Rancho Izaguirre as a recruitment centre); Infobae, 2025-03-13 (the National Guard's September 2024 operation at the ranch); Tlachinollan, "Guerrero: territorio de personas desaparecidas" (Iguala and Acapulco recoveries, prosecution rates); Human Rights Watch, 2019-01-15 (Los Otros Desaparecidos de Iguala); Proceso, 2026-04-03 (Holy Week searches); the figure of 36 sentences for forced disappearance is the CNB's count to the end of 2021, as reported in the UN Committee on Enforced Disappearances' 2022 report on Mexico. Web sources consulted 2026-07-06 unless stated; passages re-verified 2026-10-14. ↩

Where this piece says a state "redacts", it means records attributed to that state appear as CONFIDENCIAL in the federal public version; except for Jalisco, whose Fiscalía told the CNB in 2020 that none of what it sends may be published, no public document shows which office's decision produces the flag.

Named individuals. No one named in this piece was interviewed for it, and no individual is identified here from registry data. María de Jesús Solís, the families represented by Centro Prodh, and every other person named in these pages appear as they appear in the investigations cited — ZonaDocs, Quinto Elemento Lab, Data Cívica and Mexican press reports — whose reporters obtained the testimony and published the names. Quinto Elemento records that the individuals and quotations in its investigation are published with their families' participation Source [9]. Where a cited investigation does not state how consent was obtained, this piece repeats a name only because it is already public and makes no claim beyond that.

[5] Redaction over time — vintage Apr–Dec 2025. Ten pinned monthly snapshots of the mirror, upstream commit SHAs in src/version_audit.py. ↩

[6] Unidentified bodies — vintage 2006–2023. Efraín Tzuc and Mayela Sánchez, "Cierra sexenio de AMLO con más de 72,100 cuerpos sin identificar", Quinto Elemento Lab / A dónde van los desaparecidos, 2024-09-24 (investigation; data and methodology). Compiled from transparency requests to all 32 state forensic services and the FGR. A floor, not a total: Morelos declined to respond, and the count covers whole cadavers entering Semefos, excluding unindividuated remains. Not derived from any dataset in this repository and not merged with the registry figures — the overlap between the 72,172 and the 134,268 is unknown and, by construction, unknowable from public data. ↩

[7] Registry field completeness — vintage 2023-08-23. Data Cívica, "Volver a desaparecer" (project), reported by Sandra Rojas, La Cadera de Eva, 2024-03-20. Audit of the 110,964-record public RNPDNO version of 2023-08-23: reporter contact left blank in 7 of 10 records. Centro Prodh (César Contreras), quoted in the same La Cadera de Eva report, on families whose details were given and never entered. ↩

[8] Erased names — comparison of two 2023 public versions. Data Cívica, "Volver a desaparecer" (project; open data), scraped 2024-03-01; reported by Sandra Rojas, La Cadera de Eva, 2024-03-20. 10,953 names in the 110,964-record version of 2023-08-23 and absent from the 94,283-record post-census version. Data Cívica's own limit, quoted rather than softened: the comparison establishes that a record left the register, not that the person was found, alive or safe. ↩

[9] "Located" people still missing. Efraín Tzuc, "Decenas de personas 'localizadas' por el Gobierno siguen desaparecidas", Quinto Elemento Lab / A dónde van los desaparecidos, 2024-03-06 (investigation). 16,681 declared located; 11,026 names reconstructed, 4,607 redacted; crossed against collective lists, FGR "¿Has visto a...?" notices, UN CED urgent actions and dirty-war files to 85 candidates; 30 confirmed still missing by ten journalists contacting families and collectives. Also the source for the October 2023 call-centre log. Named individuals and quotations are published in that investigation with their families' participation. ↩

[10] Data Cívica, "A quienes nos faltan: sin datos para encontrarles" (fifth edition, published September 2026, after this piece's data freeze; compendium). Analyses an RNPDNO record-level extract taken in February 2026 and received in April 2026, plus statistical-version consultations of July 2024, July 2025 and July 2026. Its 38.5% confidential share is a different vintage, and possibly a different denominator, from this piece's 36.8% (133,566 unresolved records, 2 December 2025); the two are not combined. Consulted 2026-10-12. ↩

Cross-checks: category sensitivity tested (DESAPARECIDA vs +NO LOCALIZADA moves the national count +6.1%, but Zacatecas +42%); confidential records are counted as people but excluded from every field-level analysis; 15 headline numbers are recomputed automatically against the freeze on each build (data/publication_freezes/2026-08-15/derived/automated_claim_checks.csv). All figures reproduce from src/ in the project repository (https://github.com/heliog83/desaparecidos-mx). Full methodology: methodology; refresh audit and number-by-number diff: data refresh audit; source audit: source audit.
